Ego in this work means the sense of being a separate self that stands apart from life—the "I" that feels like it owns experience, decides things, and needs to protect itself. It's the narrator running commentary on what happens, the one who takes credit and blame.

In self-inquiry, you're not trying to kill the ego or get rid of it. You're looking at what it actually is. When you turn attention toward the one who feels separate, who's aware of the restlessness or the thought, what do you find?
